summary: Hydra Payments is evaluating Redwood for payments-related inference. Primary concerns: p95 latency under 120ms for short chat prompts, sustained tokens/sec at concurrency 50-200, and secure VPC/KMS for PCI adjacency. Next step: run a benchmark with Hydra prompts and compare hosted vs Dedicated (g5/a800) and confirm security artifacts.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-30 14:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Moretti (SE), Priya Rao (Solutions Eng), Samir Patel (Hydra Head of Platform), Alicia Gomez (SRE), Ravi Menon (ML Infra), Jordan Lee (CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, really appreciate you making time. Quick intro, I'm Maya, I'm the AE for Hydra, with Luca and Priya from our engineering team. How's everyone doing?
[00:12] Samir Patel: Good, thanks Maya. Busy day but excited, we wanted to dig into latency and throughput mostly.
[00:18] Maya Chen: Exactly, today's goal is to understand your p95 goals, concurrency patterns, and pick the right mode — hosted, dedicated, or private — and then agree next steps for a benchmark.
[00:29] Jordan Lee: Cool. To frame it: we're building a payments chat assistant that needs near-instant autopilot suggestions during checkout. p95 target for short prompts is around 120ms and for longer multi-turn flow maybe 400-500ms. Concurrency will vary: during peak we see ~150 concurrent sessions, typical steady at 30-50.
[00:48] Alicia Gomez: Also we need streaming support because we stream token-by-token to the web socket clients. So chunked responses and low tail latency are important.
[00:58] Luca Moretti: Great, streaming + p95 are often the friction points. Quick question on prompt lengths and tokens/sec — are you mostly short prompts like 20-90 tokens or do you have long context windows?
[01:10] Ravi Menon: Mostly short. Average prompt+reply is ~60 tokens, but for dispute resolution flows can hit 800-1,200 tokens. The 60-token fast path is the one we care about for checkout latency.
[01:23] Priya Rao: Understood. For short tokens the model and runtime choices + batching rules matter. Hosted can give you fast time-to-value, Dedicated gives predictable throughput and better p95 at scale, Private for air-gapped or strict PCI needs.
[01:36] Samir Patel: We have PCI adjacency concerns, not full card storage but logs and telemetry, so isolation/VPC is a big ask. We may need Redwood Private or Dedicated in a VPC.
[01:47] Maya Chen: Totally. We'll map that. Can you share what p95 means to you in SLA terms? Is 120ms p95 for the entire request including network?
[01:56] Jordan Lee: Ideally yes end-to-end for users in EU/US. We can tolerate a longer tail for backend analytics.
[02:05] Luca Moretti: Noted. For end-to-end we usually break down: client network + routing ~30-50ms, infra + model inference the rest. On Dedicated with optimized kernels we can often get sub-80ms p95 for short 60-token transactions on A800-style hardware, less on g5 depending on quantization.
[02:25] Alicia Gomez: A question — do you have real token/sec numbers for these setups? We need sustained tokens/sec and also tokens/sec per GPU to plan capacity.
[02:33] Priya Rao: Yes, we typically run tokens/sec benchmarks during PoC. Roughly, a single A800 (p4x? careful) — sorry, a800-class — can do X tokens/sec for 60-token prompts in fp16 and higher with quantization. I don't want to quote the wrong number but Luca can share ballpark.
[02:48] Luca Moretti: Sure. Ballpark: on fp16 a single a800 instance gives ~1,200-1,800 tokens/sec on short prompts with optimized kernels and high concurrency. With 4-bit quantization you can push higher throughput but may see small quality deltas. On g5 (NVIDIA g5) numbers are lower per GPU but cheaper; you can mitigate with more GPUs or sharding.
[03:07] Samir Patel: So to meet 150 concurrent sessions each doing a 60-token prompt every ~10s — that math is important. If each session triggers ~6 tokens per second sustained, multiply out.
[03:18] Maya Chen: Right, we can run the math and do a capacity plan. Also KV cache/prefix caching for repeated prompts can reduce work. Note: sometimes our transcripters say KP cache, so bear with that.
[03:31] Ravi Menon: (laughs) yep we've seen KP cache in other docs. More importantly, what's your approach to streaming and p95 — do you avoid batching for streaming requests?
[03:40] Priya Rao: We have intelligent batching that respects streaming SLOs. For strict p95 streaming we prioritize low-latency lanes: small micro-batches or single-request fast path. For throughput batches, we aggregate. You can tune policies per-route.
[03:53] Jordan Lee: That sounds promising. Also can Redwood fall back to a cheaper model if capacity constrained? We want graceful degradation.
[03:59] Luca Moretti: Yes, smart routing can fallback to smaller model variants; plus can route by policy (latency vs cost). For payments, we'd recommend reserve Dedicated capacity to avoid noisy-neighbor effects.
[04:12] Samir Patel: Security wise, we need SOC2, SSO, and KMS integration. Any blockers?
[04:18] Maya Chen: We have SOC2 and can provide the report. For KMS we support cloud KMS integrations and HSM via our Private offering — we'll share the docs after.
[04:27] Alicia Gomez: Also need audit logs for token-level usage for compliance.
[04:31] Priya Rao: Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and audit logs per-route. We'll include example screenshots.
[04:39] Samir Patel: Perfect. Back to p95 numbers: can you run a benchmark for our short prompts and include hosted vs Dedicated numbers and show tokens/sec?
[04:47] Luca Moretti: Absolutely. We usually run three legs: Hosted baseline, Dedicated on a800-type, and Dedicated on g5-type. We'll measure p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, and concurrency scaling. We'll also measure streaming latencies token-by-token.
[05:02] Ravi Menon: For hosted, are there regional differences? We have EU customers primarily.
[05:08] Maya Chen: Yes we have regions; routing by region helps cut network hops. For the benchmark we'll run from EU egress to EU region to be realistic.
[05:17] Jordan Lee: Can you also report cost per token at the target SLOs? We need to compare economics.
[05:22] Priya Rao: We'll include cost modeling: cost per 1M tokens at steady state and at peak with reserved capacity examples. Also suggestions like quantization and caching to reduce unit cost.
[05:33] Samir Patel: Any caveats on model compatibility with quantization? We use a customized model variant for internal fine-tune.
[05:39] Luca Moretti: Fine-tunes sometimes react differently to heavy quantization; we'll test your fine-tuned artifact if you can provide a container or model weights access via secure transfer. Otherwise we benchmark on a similar open model.
[05:51] Samir Patel: We can provide a sample fine-tuned checkpoint via a temporary S3 link under NDA.
[05:57] Maya Chen: Great, that'll make the benchmark realistic. Can we confirm the expected concurrency profile as a histogram? Peak 150, 30-50 steady, bursts to 200 for promos?
[06:07] Samir Patel: Yes that's accurate. Bursts up to 200 for flash sales.
[06:11] Priya Rao: Noted. For bursts, Dedicated autoscaling with burst capacity or pre-warming helps maintain p95. We'll propose autoscale policies.
[06:21] Alicia Gomez: Thought on observability — do you provide per-request traces integrated with our tracing backend?
[06:26] Luca Moretti: We expose tracing hooks and logs; we can integrate with common backends or push traces to your telemetry.
[06:33] Jordan Lee: Okay, last question: network latency from our infra to the cloud region can be variable. Do you support colocated Private deployments?
[06:41] Maya Chen: Yes Private on-prem or VPC peering options exist; that's typically part of an enterprise contract. We'll scope that if needed after the benchmark.
[06:50] Samir Patel: Sounds good. Let's recap next steps.
[06:54] Maya Chen: Action items: Maya send pricing and SOC2/KMS docs; Luca will run benchmarks once Samir drops prompts and the model artifact; Samir to provide prompt set and concurrency histogram; Priya to answer SSO/KMS follow-ups. We'll aim to have initial benchmark in ~1 week.
[07:10] Samir Patel: One clarification — p95 120ms end-to-end is our goal but if hosted numbers are within 150-200ms that's acceptable only if cost is substantially lower.
[07:20] Priya Rao: Understood — we'll include tradeoff charts.
[07:24] Alicia Gomez: Also include a streaming-specific p95 metric (time to first token and time to last token) — we care about time-to-first-token for user perceived latency.
[07:33] Luca Moretti: We'll measure TTF (time-to-first) and per-token deltas in the benchmark.
[07:38] Jordan Lee: Great. That should cover it for now.
[07:41] Maya Chen: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the deck and benchmark plan. Any other questions?
[07:45] Ravi Menon: No, thanks. Looking forward to the numbers.
[07:48] Maya Chen: Ok we'll send the invites for the deep dive after we have results. Bye everyone.

Notes on transcript: occasional mis-hearings e.g., KP cache for KV cache, a800-class sometimes noted as A eight hundred, and some overlaps in speaker labels.

References shared during call: link: /redwood/decks/latency-benchmarks (shared by Maya), link: /security/soc2-redwood (shared by Maya), Benchmarks spreadsheet (Luca will populate).

End of transcript.
